## Proof

Let $A$ be a countably infinite set and $r$ a complete, transitive relation on $A$.

**Step 1: $r$ is a total preorder.**

Completeness with $a=b$ gives $a\,r\,a$, so $r$ is reflexive. Define an equivalence relation on $A$ by
$$a \sim b \iff (a\,r\,b \text{ and } b\,r\,a).$$
Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate; transitivity of $\sim$ follows from transitivity of $r$. Let $A/{\sim}$ denote the set of equivalence classes, and define
$$[a] \preceq [b] \iff a\,r\,b.$$

This is well defined: if $a\sim a'$ and $b\sim b'$, then $a\,r\,b \Rightarrow a'\,r\,a\,r\,b\,r\,b' \Rightarrow a'\,r\,b'$, and the converse is symmetric. Completeness of $r$ gives totality of $\preceq$, transitivity is inherited, and antisymmetry holds because $[a]\preceq[b]$ and $[b]\preceq[a]$ force $a\sim b$, i.e. $[a]=[b]$. Hence $(A/{\sim},\preceq)$ is a **linear order**. Since $A$ is countable, $A/{\sim}$ is countable.

**Step 2: Every countable linear order embeds into $\mathbb{Q}$.**

Enumerate $A/{\sim}=\{c_1,c_2,c_3,\dots\}$. We construct an order-embedding $g:A/{\sim}\to\mathbb{Q}$ inductively. Suppose $g(c_1),\dots,g(c_{n-1})$ have been assigned distinct rationals so that for all $i,j<n$,
$$c_i \preceq c_j \iff g(c_i)\le g(c_j). \tag{$\ast$}$$

Consider $c_n$. Among $\{c_1,\dots,c_{n-1}\}$, let
$$L=\{c_k:k<n,\; c_k\prec c_n\}, \qquad U=\{c_k:k<n,\; c_n\prec c_k\}.$$
By the inductive hypothesis $(\ast)$, every element of $g(L)$ is strictly below every element of $g(U)$. If $L\neq\emptyset$, let $\alpha=\max g(L)$; otherwise let $\alpha=-\infty$ conceptually (pick any rational below all of $g(U)$, or just any rational if $U=\emptyset$ too). If $U\neq\emptyset$, let $\beta=\min g(U)$; otherwise pick any rational above $\alpha$. Because $\mathbb{Q}$ is dense and $g(L),g(U)$ are finite, the interval $(\alpha,\beta)\cap\mathbb{Q}$ is nonempty. Assign $g(c_n)$ to any rational in this interval.

This choice guarantees $c_k\prec c_n \iff g(c_k)<g(c_n)$ and $c_n\prec c_k \iff g(c_n)<g(c_k)$ for every $k<n$, so $(\ast)$ is preserved for all pairs among $\{c_1,\dots,c_n\}$. By induction we obtain $g$ defined on all of $A/{\sim}$ satisfying $(\ast)$ for every pair — an order-embedding.

**Step 3: Build $f$.**

Define $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ by $f(a)=g([a])$. Then for any $a,b\in A$,
$$a\,r\,b \iff [a]\preceq[b] \iff g([a])\le g([b]) \iff f(a)\ge f(b),$$
where the last equivalence uses that $g$ is an order-embedding (so $\preceq$ is exactly reflected by $\le$ on the values). Thus $a\,r\,b$ if and only if $f(a)\ge f(b)$.

Therefore such a function $f$ must exist. $\blacksquare$
